intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 gene (also known as peripherin/RDS) on chromosome 6p. Digenic RP7 is caused by double heterozygosity for mutations in the PRPH2 gene and the ROM1 gene. Homozygous mutation in PRPH2 has been found in patients with Leber congenital amaurosis or juvenile retinitis pigmentosa.

checks.evidence_quote: We report here three mutations of the human homologue of the rds gene (RDS) that cosegregate with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa in separate families.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports RDS mutations causing autosomal dominant RP. It does not state zygosity (heterozygous) or use the RP7 designation, though dominant inheritance implies heterozygosity.

checks.evidence_quote: Three families were identified with mutations in the unlinked photoreceptor-specific genes ROM1 and peripherin/RDS, in which only double heterozygotes develop retinitis pigmentosa (RP).
checks.explanation: The paper describes digenic RP in double heterozygotes for peripherin/RDS (PRPH2) and ROM1. The label RP7 is OMIM nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is a form of retinitis pigmentosa, a hereditary retinal degeneration characterized by degeneration of the photoreceptors, that is caused by mutation in the gene encoding the photoreceptor-specific glycoprotein peripherin/RDS (Kajiwara et al., 1991; Farrar et al., 1991). The disorder is usually transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait, and onset may be late (Farrar et al., 1991; Jordan et al., 1992). A digenic form occurs in individuals who are double heterozygotes for mutations in PRPH2 and ROM1 (Kajiwara et al., 1994). PRPH2 mutations cause highly variable phenotypes, even within a single family, including retinitis pigmentosa, pattern macular dystrophy, and fundus flavimaculatus (Weleber et al., 1993; Manes et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Weleber et al. (1993) reported 3 separate phenotypes within a single family carrying a 3-bp deletion of codon 153 or 154 of the PRPH2 gene. The mother presented at age 63 years with a profoundly abnormal electroretinogram (ERG) and adult-onset retinitis pigmentosa that progressed dramatically over 12 years, with marked loss of peripheral visual field. One daughter developed pattern macular dystrophy at age 31 years; at age 44 years her ERG was moderately abnormal but her clinical disease was limited to the macula. Another daughter presented at age 42 years with macular degeneration and over 10 years developed the clinical picture of fundus flavimaculatus; her peripheral visual field was preserved but her ERG was moderately abnormal. The son had onset of macular degeneration at age 44 years, with pericentral scotomas and a markedly abnormal ERG; fluorescein angiography revealed punctate pigment epithelial transmission defects.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2013) described 3 patients homozygous for PRPH2 mutations who had a clinical diagnosis of Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) (2 patients) or juvenile RP (1 patient). All had visual impairment within the first year of life, nondetectable or reduced ERGs, and a very similar form of maculopathy in the fundus; the 2 LCA patients had nystagmus. Fundus photography of one patient showed a prominent multilobulated central atrophic maculopathy surrounded by concentric rings of yellow deposits, with vessel narrowing and fine diffuse peripheral retinal changes; another showed pigment deposits peripherally and in the macular region, extensive disease with choroidal sclerosis, vessel narrowing, optic disc pallor, and a central extensive atrophic maculopathy, with unusual globular lesions in the foveal region on optical coherence tomography (OCT). The third patient had diffuse retinal dystrophy with retinal vessel narrowing, retinal pigment epithelium mottling and loss, and a multilobulated maculopathy, with fairly good visual acuity (20/40). In contrast, heterozygous family members were asymptomatic but showed detectable maculopathy: the 56-year-old father of one patient had macular pattern dystrophy with essentially normal visual acuity, and the 57-year-old mother of another patient had 20/20 visual acuity but a florid butterfly-shaped macular pattern dystrophy and retinal flecks.

paragraphs.text: Manes et al. (2015) studied the clinical features of adRP patients with PRPH2 mutations from French families. The clinical severity was moderate, with 78% of eyes having 1-0.5 visual acuity and 52% of eyes retaining more than 50% of the visual field. Some patients characteristically showed vitelliform deposits or macular involvement. In some families, pericentral RP or macular dystrophy was found in some family members while widespread RP was present in other members of the same family. Manes et al. (2015) concluded that PRPH2 mutations cause highly variable phenotypes and moderate forms of adRP, including mild cases that could be underdiagnosed.
